Africa stands at a pivotal juncture, where the energy transition and digital transformation are not just parallel trends; they are converging revolutions to unlock a new development paradigm.
 
Across Africa, more than 2,000 languages are spoken, with 75 of them having over a million speakers. Yet the AI systems already shaping markets, education, and public services are trained to recognize only a few. This is not just a technical gap; it’s a political one. When technology doesn’t speak your language, it can’t serve your future. That’s why localizing innovation - from data to design - is foundational.
 
Today, at the 2025 Oxford Africa Conference, I had the privilege to reflect on how AI and data technologies can become powerful enablers for a just and inclusive energy transition in Africa. The continent holds over 60% of global solar potential, 30% of the world’s critical mineral reserves, and a youth demographic poised to drive innovation and growth. Yet unlocking this potential requires more than ambition; it demands intentional design, inclusive architecture, and integrated systems:
 
1️⃣ Design for inclusion from the start: Across Africa, MSMEs make up 90% of businesses and 80% of employment. Yet they remain underserved by digital and energy infrastructure. AI systems must be built on local data, adapted to diverse operating contexts and geared toward inclusive growth. Digital tools, when intentionally designed, can extend services and financing to the last mile—turning technology into an equalizer, not a divider.
 
2️⃣ Co-develop digital and energy infrastructure: Energy and AI are not parallel tracks; they are co-dependent systems. We must invest in digital infrastructure powered by renewables and in energy systems optimized by AI. Africa currently accounts for just 1% of global data center capacity, but needs over 700 new centers by 2030. These should be clean-powered, locally managed, and embedded in national development strategies.
 
3️⃣ Move up the value chain in clean technologies: Despite holding 30% of the world’s critical minerals, the continent continues to export raw materials and re-import finished technologies at many times the cost. The future lies in integrated value chains: from mining and processing to battery manufacturing and renewable-powered digital infrastructure. The DRC–Zambia battery corridor offers a model for regionally coordinated value creation.
 
We have the innovation. We have the tools. Now we need to scale them and embed them into the heart of development strategies. The convergence of AI and clean energy isn’t just an opportunity; it’s a catalyst to redefine development outcomes across Africa.
 
The question is no longer whether Africa can lead, but how we ensure that leadership is equitable, sustainable, and strategically designed.
